jagannath: A particular form of Vishnu, or of Krishna, whose chief idol and worship are at Puri, in Orissa. The idol is considered to contain the bones of Krishna and to possess a soul. The principal festivals are the Snanayatra, when the idol is bathed, and the Rathayatra, when the image is drawn upon a car adorned with obscene paintings.
jacobin: 1. (Eccl. Hist.) A Dominican friar; -- so named because, before the French Revolution, that order had a convent in the Rue St. Jacques, Paris. 2. One of a society of violent agitators in France, during the revolution of 1789, who held secret meetings in the Jacobin convent in the Rue St.
jargonic: Of or pertaining to the mineral jargon.
jacobaeanlily: A bulbous plant (Amaryllis, or Sprekelia, formosissima) from Mexico. It bears a single, large, deep, red, lilylike flower. [Written also Jacobean.]
jacksmith: A smith who makes jacks. See 2d Jack, 4, c. Dryden.
jards: A callous tumor on the leg of a horse, below the hock.
jacqueminot: A half-hardy, deep crimson rose of the remontant class; -- so named after General Jacqueminot, of France.
janusfaced: Double-faced; deceitful. Janus-faced lock, one having duplicate faces so as to go upon a right or a left hand door, the key entering on either side indifferently. Knight.
jangling: Producing discordant sounds. "A jangling noise." Milton. | 1. Idle babbling; vain disputation. From which some, having swerved, have turned aside unto vain jangling. 1 Tim. i. 6. 2. Wrangling; altercation. Lamb.
jar: A turn. [Only in phrase.] On the jar, on the turn, ajar, as a door. | 1. A deep, broad-mouthed vessel of earthenware or glass, for holding fruit, preserves, etc., or for ornamental purposes; as, a jar of honey; a rose jar. Dryden. 2.
jantu: A machine of great antiquity, used in Bengal for raising water to irrigate land. Knight.
jailer: The keeper of a jail or prison. [Written also jailor, gaoler.]
jambes: In the Middle Ages, armor for the legs below the knees. [Written also giambeux.] Chaucer.
jackeen: A drunken, dissolute fellow. [Ireland] S. C. Hall.
jackman: 1. One wearing a jack; a horse soldier; a retainer. See 3d Jack, n. Christie . . . the laird's chief jackman. Sir W. Scott. 2. A cream cheese. (old) Sir T. Elyot. JACK-O'-LANTERN Jack"-o'-lan`tern, n. See Jack-with-a-lantern, under 2d Jack. JACKPOT Jackpot 1. (a) See "jack pot" under jack;
jamaica: One of the West India is islands. Jamaica ginger, a variety of ginger, called also white ginger, prepared in Jamaica from the best roots, which are deprived of their epidermis and dried separately. -- Jamaica pepper, allspice. -- Jamaica rose (Bot.), a West Indian melastomaceous shrub (Blakea trinervis), with showy pink flowers.
jackal: 1. (Zoöl.) Any one of several species of carnivorous animals inhabiting Africa and Asia, related to the dog and wolf. They are cowardly, nocturnal, and gregarious. They feed largely on carrion, and are noted for their piercing and dismal howling. Note: The common species of Southern Asia (Canis aureus) is yellowish gray, varied with brown on the shoulders, haunches, and legs.
jawfall: Depression of the jaw; hence, depression of spirits. M. Griffith (1660).
jambooree: A noisy or unrestrained carousal or frolic; a spree. [Slang] Kipling. A Calcutta-made pony cart had been standing in front of the manager's bungalow when Raja Singh started on his jamboree. W. A. Fraser.
jacobitism: The principles of the Jacobites. Mason.
jacquerie: The name given to a revolt of French peasants against the nobles in 1358, the leader assuming the contemptuous title, Jacques Bonhomme, given by the nobles to the peasantry. Hence, any revolt of peasants.
japancurrent: A branch of the equatorial current of the Pacific, washing the eastern coast of Formosa and thence flowing northeastward past Japan and merging into the easterly drift of the North Pacific; -- called also Kuro-Siwo, or Black Stream, in allusion to the deep blue of its water. It is similar in may ways to the Gulf Stream.
jacana: Any of several wading birds belonging to the genus Jacana and several allied genera, all of which have spurs on the wings. They are able to run about over floating water weeds by means of their very long, spreading toes. Called also surgeon bird. Note: The most common South American species is Jacana spinosa.
jakie: A South American striped frog (Pseudis paradoxa), remarkable for having a tadpole larger than the adult, and hence called also paradoxical frog.
jahwist: The author of the passages of the Old Testament, esp. those of the Hexateuch, in which God is styled Yahweh, or Jehovah; the author of the Yahwistic, or Jehovistic, Prophetic Document (J); also, the document itself.
jacky: (a) A landsman's nickname for a seaman, resented by the latter. (b) English gin. [Dial. Eng.]
jail: A kind of prison; a building for the confinement of persons held in lawful custody, especially for minor offenses or with reference to some future judicial proceeding. | To imprison. T. Adams (1614). [Bolts] that jail you from free life. Tennyson.
jararaca: A poisonous serpent of Brazil (Bothrops jararaca), about eighteen inches long, and of a dusky, brownish color, variegated with red and black spots.
jagger: One who carries about a small load; a peddler. See 2d Jag. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott. | One who, or that which, jags; specifically: (a) jagging iron used for crimping pies, cakes, etc. (b) A toothed chisel. See Jag, v. t. Jagger spring, a spring beneath a seat, and resting on cleats or…
jahvist: The author of the passages of the Old Testament, esp. those of the Hexateuch, in which God is styled Yahweh, or Jehovah; the author of the Yahwistic, or Jehovistic, Prophetic Document (J); also, the document itself.
jargle: To emit a harsh or discordant sound. (old) Bp. Hall.
jacchus: The common marmoset (Hapale vulgaris). Formerly, the name was also applied to other species of the same genus.
jangler: 1. An idle talker; a babbler; a prater. Chaucer. 2. A wrangling, noisy fellow.
jaspideous: Consisting of jasper, or containing jasper; jaspery; jasperlike.
jasmine: A shrubby plant of the genus Jasminum, bearing flowers of a peculiarly fragrant odor. The J. officinale, common in the south of Europe, bears white flowers. The Arabian jasmine is J. Sambac, and, with J. angustifolia, comes from the East Indies. The yellow false jasmine in the Gelseminum sempervirens (see Gelsemium).
japanner: 1. One who varnishes in the manner of the Japanese, or one skilled in the art. 2. A bootblack.
jagannatha: A particular form of Vishnu, or of Krishna, whose chief idol and worship are at Puri, in Orissa. The idol is considered to contain the bones of Krishna and to possess a soul. The principal festivals are the Snanayatra, when the idol is bathed, and the Rathayatra, when the image is drawn upon a car adorned with obscene paintings.
javelin: A sort of light spear, to be thrown or cast by thew hand; anciently, a weapon of war used by horsemen and foot soldiers; now used chiefly in hunting the wild boar and other fierce game. | To pierce with a javelin. Tennyson.
jackslave: A low servant; a mean fellow. Shak.
janizary: A soldier of a privileged military class, which formed the nucleus of the Turkish infantry, but was suppressed in 1826. [written also janissary.]
jarvy: 1. The driver of a hackney coach. [Slang, Eng.] Carlyle. 2. A hackney coach. [Slang, Eng.] The litter at the bottom of the jarvy. T. Hook.
javelinier: A soldier armed with a javelin. Holland.
jay: Any one of the numerous species of birds belonging to Garrulus, Cyanocitta, and allied genera. They are allied to the crows, but are smaller, more graceful in form, often handsomely colored, and usually have a crest. Note: The European jay (Garrulus glandarius) is a large and handsomely colored species, having the body pale reddish brown, lighter beneath;
jackalent: A small stuffed puppet to be pelted in Lent; hence, a simple fellow.
jaw: 1. (Anat.) (a) One of the bones, usually bearing teeth, which form the framework of the mouth. (b) Hence, also, the bone itself with the teeth and covering. (c) In the plural, the mouth. 2. | To scold; to clamor. [Law] Smollett.
jarringly: In a jarring or discordant manner.
jardiniere: An ornamental stand or receptacle for plants, flowers, etc., used as a piece of decorative furniture in room.
jalapin: A glucoside found in the stems of the jalap plant and scammony. It is a strong purgative.
jaggery: Raw palm sugar, made in the East Indies by evaporating the fresh juice of several kinds of palm trees, but specifically that of the palmyra (Borassus flabelliformis). [Written also jagghery.]
jackketch: A public executioner, or hangman. [Eng.] The manor of Tyburn was formerly held by Richard Jaquett, where felons for a long time were executed; from whence we have Jack Ketch. Lloyd's MS., British Museum.
jackanapes: 1. A monkey; an ape. Shak. 2. A coxcomb; an impertinent or conceited fellow. A young upstart jackanapes. Arbuthnot.
jackknife: A large, strong clasp knife for the pocket; a pocket knife. JACK-'-LANTERN Jack"-o'-lan`tern, n. See Jack-with-a-lantern, under 2d Jack.
jacobinic: Of or pertaining to the Jacobins of France; revolutionary; of the nature of, or characterized by, Jacobinism. Burke. -- Jac`o*bin"ic*al*ly, adv.
jargonist: One addicted to jargon; one who uses cant or slang. Macaulay.
japanese: Of or pertaining to Japan, or its inhabitants. | 1. A native or inhabitant of Japan; collectively, the people of Japan. 2. sing. The language of the people of Japan.
jaspilite: A compact siliceous rock resembling jasper.
jabot: 1. Originally, a kind of ruffle worn by men on the bosom of the shirt. 2. An arrangement of lace or tulle, looped ornamentally, and worn by women on the front of the dress.
jansenist: A follower of Cornelius Jansen, a Roman Catholic bishop of Ypres, in Flanders, in the 17th century, who taught certain doctrines denying free will and the possibility of resisting divine grace.
japanned: Treated, or coated, with varnish in the Japanese manner. Japanned leather,leather treated with coatings of Japan varnish, and dried in a stove. Knight.
jarring: Shaking; disturbing; discordant. "A jarring sound." Dryden. | 1. A shaking; a tremulous motion; as, the jarring of a steamship, caused by its engines. 2. Discord; a clashing of interests. "Endless jarrings and immortal hate." Dryden.
jaunt: 1. To ramble here and there; to stroll; to make an excursion. 2. To ride on a jaunting car. Jaunting car, a kind of low-set open vehicle, used in Ireland, in which the passengers ride sidewise,… | To jolt; to jounce. (old) Bale.
jaguapalm: A great Brazilian palm (Maximiliana regia), having immense spathes which are used for baskets and tubs.
japannish: After the manner of the Japanese; resembling japanned articles. Carlyle.
jaggy: Having jags; set with teeth; notched; uneven; as, jaggy teeth. Addison.
janeofapes: A silly, pert girl; -- corresponding to jackanapes. Massinger.
jamestownweed: The poisonous thorn apple or stramonium (Datura stramonium), a rank weed early noticed at Jamestown, Virginia. See Datura. Note: This name is often corrupted into jimson, jimpson, and gympsum.
jab: To thrust; to stab; to punch. See Job, v. t. [Scot. & Colloq. U. S.] | A thrust or stab. [Scot. & Colloq. U. S.]
jape: To jest; to play tricks; to jeer. (old) Chaucer. | To mock; to trick. Chaucer. I have not been putting a jape upon you. Sir W. Scott. The coy giggle of the young lady to whom he has imparted his latest merry jape. W. Besant.
jackass: 1. The male ass; a donkey. 2. A conceited dolt; a perverse blockhead. Jackass bark (Naut.), a three-masted vessel, with only the foremast square-rigged; a barkentine. -- Jackass deer (Zoöl.), the koba. -- Jackass hare, Jackass rabbit (Zoöl.). See Jack rabbit, under 2d Jack, n.
jackscrew: A jack in which a screw is used for lifting, or exerting pressure. See Illust. of 2d Jack, n., 5.
jain: One of a numerous sect in British India, holding the tenets of Jainism.
jager: 1. (Mil.) A sharpshooter. See Yager. 2. (Zoöl.) Any species of gull of the genus Stercorarius. Three species occur on the Atlantic coast. The jagers pursue other species of gulls and force them to disgorge their prey. The two middle tail feathers are usually decidedly longer than the rest. Called also boatswain, and marline-spike bird.
jaborandi: The native name of a South American rutaceous shrub (Pilocarpus pennatifolius). The leaves are used in medicine as an diaphoretic and sialogogue.
jasperize: To convert into, or make to resemble, jasper. Polished specimens of jasperized and agatized woods. Pop. Sci. Monthly.
jagged: Having jags; having rough, sharp notches, protuberances, or teeth; cleft; laciniate; divided; as, jagged rocks. " Jagged vine leaves' shade." Trench. -- Jag"ged*ly, adv. -- Jag"ged*ness, n.
jackeroo: A young man living as an apprentice on a sheep station, or otherwise engaged in acquainting himself with colonial life. [Colloq., Australia]
jaspidean: Consisting of jasper, or containing jasper; jaspery; jasperlike.
jaunty: Airy; showy; finical; hence, characterized by an affected or fantastical manner.
jazerant: A coat of defense made of small plates of metal sewed upon linen or the like; also, this kind of armor taken generally; as, a coat of jazerant.
jaconet: A thin cotton fabric, between and muslin, used for dresses, neckcloths, etc. [Written also jacconet.]
javanese: Of or pertaining to Java, or to the people of Java. -- n. sing. & pl. A native or natives of Java.
jan: One of intermediate order between angels and men.
jacobinize: To taint with, or convert to, Jacobinism. France was not then jacobinized. Burke.
jacobian: Of or pertaining to a style of architecture and decoration in the time of James the First, of England. "A Jacobean table." C. L. Eastlake.
jasponyx: An onyx, part or all of whose layers consist of jasper.
jambul: The Java plum; also, a drug obtained from its bark and seeds, used as a remedy for diabetes.
jackstone: (a) One of the pebbles or pieces used in the game of jackstones. (b) (pl.) A game played with five small stones or pieces of metal. See 6th Chuck.
japan: Work varnished and figured in the Japanese manner; also, the varnish or lacquer used in japanning. | Of or pertaining to Japan, or to the lacquered work of that country; as, Japan ware. Japan allspice (Bot.), a spiny shrub from Japan (Chimonanthus fragrans), related to the Carolina allspice.
japonism: A quality, idiom, or peculiarity characteristic of the Japanese or their products, esp. in art.
jambeux: In the Middle Ages, armor for the legs below the knees. [Written also giambeux.] Chaucer.
jauntiness: The quality of being jaunty. That jauntiness of air I was once master of. Addison.
jaalgoat: A species of wild goat (Capra Nubiana) found in the mountains of Abyssinia, Upper Egypt, and Arabia; -- called also beden, and jaela.
janizarian: Of or pertaining to the janizaries, or their government. Burke.
jabiru: One of several large wading birds of the genera Mycteria and Xenorhynchus, allied to the storks in form and habits. Note: The American jabiru (Mycteria Americana) is white, with the head and neck black and nearly bare of feathers.
jalons: Long poles, topped with wisps of straw, used as landmarks and signals. Farrow.
jade: A stone, commonly of a pale to dark green color but sometimes whitish. It is very hard and compact, capable of fine polish, and is used for ornamental purposes and for implements, esp. | 1. A mean or tired horse; a worthless nag. Chaucer. Tired as a jade in overloaden cart. Sir P. Sidney. 2. A disreputable or vicious woman; a wench; a quean; also, sometimes, a worthless man. Shak.
jacketed: Wearing, or furnished with, a jacket.
jargonelle: A variety of pear which ripens early.
jako: An African parrot (Psittacus erithacus), very commonly kept as a cage bird; -- called also gray parrot.
jalousied: Furnished with jalousies; as, jalousied porches.
jacobus: An English gold coin, of the value of twenty-five shillings sterling, struck in the reign of James I.
jacobitical: Of or pertaining to the Jacobites; characterized by Jacobitism. -- Jac`o*bit"ic*al*ly, adv.
japanning: The art or act of varnishing in the Japanese manner.
jansenism: The doctrine of Jansen regarding free will and divine grace.
january: The first month of the year, containing thirty-one days. Note: Before the adoption of New Style, the commencement of the year was usually reckoned from March 25.
jacobinical: Of or pertaining to the Jacobins of France; revolutionary; of the nature of, or characterized by, Jacobinism. Burke. -- Jac`o*bin"ic*al*ly, adv.
jambolana: A myrtaceous tree of the West Indies and tropical America (Calyptranthes Jambolana), with astringent bark, used for dyeing. It bears an edible fruit.
jacquard: Pertaining to, or invented by, Jacquard, a French mechanician, who died in 1834. Jacquard apparatus or arrangement, a device applied to looms for weaving figured goods, consisting of mechanism controlled by a chain of variously perforated cards, which cause the warp threads to be lifted in the proper succession for producing the required figure.
jacobean: Of or pertaining to a style of architecture and decoration in the time of James the First, of England. "A Jacobean table." C. L. Eastlake.
japhetic: Pertaining to, or derived from, Japheth, one of the sons of Noah; as, Japhetic nations, the nations of Europe and Northern Asia; Japhetic languages.
janus: A Latin deity represented with two faces looking in opposite directions. Numa is said to have dedicated to Janus the covered passage at Rome, near the Forum, which is usually called the Temple of Janus. This passage was open in war and closed in peace. Dr. W. Smith.
jamaican: Of or pertaining to Jamaica. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Jamaica.
jatrophic: Of or pertaining to physic nuts, the seeds of plants of the genus Jatropha.
japonica: A species of Camellia (Camellia Japonica), a native of Japan, bearing beautiful red or white flowers. Many other genera have species of the same name.
janker: A long pole on two wheels, used in hauling logs. [Scot.] Jamieson.
jambool: The Java plum; also, a drug obtained from its bark and seeds, used as a remedy for diabetes.
jarrah: The mahoganylike wood of the Australian Eucalyptus marginata. See Eucalyptus.
jaghir: A village or district the government and revenues of which are assigned to some person, usually in consideration of some service to be rendered, esp. the maintenance of troops. [Written also jaghire, jagir, etc.] [India] Whitworth.
jasper: An opaque, impure variety of quartz, of red, yellow, and other dull colors, breaking with a smooth surface. It admits of a high polish, and is used for vases, seals, snuff boxes, etc. When the colors are in stripes or bands, it is called striped or banded jasper. The Egyptian pebble is a brownish yellow jasper. Jasper opal, a yellow variety of opal resembling jasper.
jack: A large tree, the Artocarpus integrifolia, common in the East Indies, closely allied to the breadfruit, from which it differs in having its leaves entire. The fruit is of great size, weighing from… | 1. A familiar nickname of, or substitute for, John. You are John Rugby, and you are Jack Rugby. Shak. 2. An impertinent or silly fellow; a simpleton; a boor; a clown; also, a servant; a rustic.
jaculator: 1. One who throws or casts. 2. (Zoöl.) The archer fish (Toxotes jaculator).
jaunce: To ride hard; to jounce. (old) Spurr'd, galled and tired by jauncing Bolingbroke. Shak.
jawed: Having jaws; -- chiefly in composition; as, lantern-jawed. "Jawed like a jetty." Skelton.
jaguarondi: A South American wild cat (Felis jaguarondi), having a long, slim body and very short legs. Its color is grayish brown, varied with a blackish hue. It is arboreal in its habits and feeds mostly on birds.
jalap: The tubers of the Mexican plant Ipomoea purga (or Exogonium purga), a climber much like the morning-glory. The abstract, extract, and powder, prepared from the tubers, are well known purgative medicines. Other species of Ipomoea yield several inferior kinds of jalap, as the I. Orizabensis, and I. tuberosa.
jayhawker: A name given to a free-booting, unenlisted, armed man or guerrilla. Note: [A term of opprobrium used in the war of 1861-65, U. S.]
jahveh: A modern transliteration of the Hebrew word translated Jehovah in the Bible; -- used by some critics to discriminate the tribal god of the ancient Hebrews from the Christian Jehovah. Yahweh or Yahwe is the spelling now generally adopted by scholars.
jacobitic: Of or pertaining to the Jacobites; characterized by Jacobitism. -- Jac`o*bit"ic*al*ly, adv.
jacket: 1. A short upper garment, extending downward to the hips; a short coat without skirts. 2. An outer covering for anything, esp. a covering of some nonconducting material such as wood or felt, used to… | 1. To put a jacket on; to furnish, as a boiler, with a jacket. 2. To thrash; to beat. [Low]
jahve: A modern transliteration of the Hebrew word translated Jehovah in the Bible; -- used by some critics to discriminate the tribal god of the ancient Hebrews from the Christian Jehovah. Yahweh or Yahwe is the spelling now generally adopted by scholars.
jamesonite: A steel-gray mineral, of metallic luster, commonly fibrous massive. It is a sulphide of antimony and lead, with a little iron. JAMES'S POWDER James"'s pow`der. (Med.) Antimonial powder, first prepared by Dr. James, ar English physician; -- called also fever powder.
jacobinism: The principles of the Jacobins; violent and factious opposition to legitimate government. Under this new stimulus, Burn's previous Jacobitism passed towards the opposite, but not very distant, extreme of Jacobinism. J. C. Shairp.
jasey: A wig; -- so called, perhaps, from being made of, or resembling, Jersey yarn. Thackeray.
jargon: Confused, unintelligible language; gibberish; hence, an artificial idiom or dialect; cant language; slang. "A barbarous jargon." Macaulay. "All jargon of the schools." Prior. | To utter jargon; to emit confused or unintelligible sounds; to talk unintelligibly, or in a harsh and noisy manner. The noisy jay, Jargoning like a foreigner at his food. Longfellow.
jane: 1. A coin of Genoa; any small coin. Chaucer. 2. A kind of twilled cotton cloth. See Jean.
jacal: In Mexico and the southwestern United States, a kind of plastered house or hut, usually made by planting poles or timber in the ground, filling in between them with screen work or wickerwork, and daubing one or both sides with mud or adobe mortar; also, this method of construction.
jaborine: An alkaloid found in jaborandi leaves, from which it is extracted as a white amorphous substance. In its action it resembles atropine.
jaggerypalm: An East Indian palm (Caryota urens) having leaves pinnate with wedge-shaped divisions, the petiole very stout. It is the principal source of jaggery, and is often cultivated for ornament.
java: 1. One of the islands of the Malay Archipelago belonging to the Netherlands. 2. Java coffee, a kind of coffee brought from Java. Java cat (Zoöl.), the musang. -- Java sparrow (Zoöl.), a species of finch (Padda oryzivora), native of Java, but very commonly kept as a cage bird; -- called also ricebird, and paddy bird.
jactitation: 1. (Law) Vain boasting or assertions repeated to the prejudice of another's right; false claim. Mozley & W. 2. (Med.) A frequent tossing or moving of the body; restlessness, as in delirium. Dunglison. Jactitation of marriage (Eng. Eccl. Law), a giving out or boasting by a party that he or she is married to another, whereby a common reputation of their matrimony may ensue.
jadish: 1. Vicious; ill-tempered; resembling a jade; -- applied to a horse. 2. Unchaste; -- applied to a woman. L'Estrange.
jawing: Scolding; clamorous or abusive talk. [Slang] H. Kingsley.
jaspery: Of the nature of jasper; mixed with jasper.
jarosite: An ocher-yellow mineral occurring on minute rhombohedral crystals. It is a hydrous sulphate of iron and potash.
jarvey: 1. The driver of a hackney coach. [Slang, Eng.] Carlyle. 2. A hackney coach. [Slang, Eng.] The litter at the bottom of the jarvy. T. Hook.
jackwood: Wood of the jack (Artocarpus integrifolia), used in cabinetwork.
jasperated: mixed with jasper; containing particles of jasper; as, jasperated agate.
jacksnipe: (a) A small European snipe (Limnocryptes gallinula); -- called also judcock, jedcock, juddock, jed, and half snipe. (b) A small American sandpiper (Tringa maculata); -- called also pectoral sandpiper, and grass snipe.
jamaicine: An alkaloid said to be contained in the bark of Geoffroya inermis, a leguminous tree growing in Jamaica and Surinam; -- called also jamacina. Watts.
jamb: 1. (Arch) The vertical side of any opening, as a door or fireplace; hence, less properly, any narrow vertical surface of wall, as the of a chimney-breast or of a pier, as distinguished from its face. Gwilt. 2. (Mining) Any thick mass of rock which prevents miners from following the lode or vein.
jacaranda: (a) The native Brazilian name for certain leguminous trees, which produce the beautiful woods called king wood, tiger wood, and violet wood. (b) A genus of bignoniaceous Brazilian trees with showy trumpet- shaped flowers.
jarl: A chief; an earl; in English history, one of the leaders in the Danish and Norse invasions. Longfellow.
jangle: 1. To sound harshly or discordantly, as bells out of tune. 2. To talk idly; to prate; to babble; to chatter; to gossip. "Thou janglest as a jay." Chaucer. 3. To quarrel in words; to altercate; | To cause to sound harshly or inharmoniously; to produce discordant sounds with. Like sweet bells jangled, out of tune, and harsh. Shak.
jaculation: The act of tossing, throwing, or hurling, as spears. Hurled to and fro with jaculation dire. Milton.
jacobite: 1. (Eng. Hist.) A partisan or adherent of James the Second, after his abdication, or of his descendants, an opposer of the revolution in 1688 in favor of William and Mary. Macaulay. 2. | Of or pertaining to the Jacobites.
jam: 1. To press into a close or tight position; to crowd; to squeeze; to wedge in. The . . . jammed in between two rocks. De Foe. 2. To crush or bruise; as, to jam a finger in the crack of a door. | 1. A mass of people or objects crowded together; also, the pressure from a crowd; a crush; as, a jam in a street; a jam of logs in a river. 2. An injury caused by jamming. [Colloq.]
jaguar: A large and powerful feline animal (Felis onca), ranging from Texas and Mexico to Patagonia. It is usually brownish yellow, with large, dark, somewhat angular rings, each generally inclosing one or two dark spots. It is chiefly arboreal in its habits. Called also the American tiger.
jactation: A throwing or tossing of the body; a shaking or agitation. Sir. W. Temple.
jainism: The heterodox Hindoo religion, of which the most striking features are the exaltation of saints or holy mortals, called jins, above the ordinary Hindoo gods, and the denial of the divine origin and infallibility of the Vedas. It is intermediate between Brahmanism and Buddhism, having some things in common with each.
jaculatory: Darting or throwing out suddenly; also, suddenly thrown out; uttered in short sentences; ejaculatory; as, jaculatory prayers. Smart.
jawbone: The bone of either jaw; a maxilla or a mandible.
jackaroo: A young man living as an apprentice on a sheep station, or otherwise engaged in acquainting himself with colonial life. [Colloq., Australia] | To be a jackaroo; to pass one's time as a jackaroo. [Colloq., Australia]
jarble: To wet; to bemire. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
jaina: One of a numerous sect in British India, holding the tenets of Jainism.
jabber: To talk rapidly, indistinctly, or unintelligibly; to utter gibberish or nonsense; to chatter. Swift. | To utter rapidly or indistinctly; to gabble; as, to jabber French. Addison.
jacob: A Hebrew patriarch (son of Isaac, and ancestor of the Jews), who in a vision saw a ladder reaching up to heaven (Gen. xxviii. 12); -- also called Israel. And Jacob said . . . with my staff I passed over this Jordan, and now I am become two bands. Gen. xxxii. 9, 10. Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel. Gen. xxxii. 28. Jacob's ladder.
jamdani: A silk fabric, with a woven pattern of sprigs of flowers. [Written also jamdanee.] Balfour (Cyc. of India).
jaundice: A morbid condition, characterized by yellowness of the eyes, skin, and urine, whiteness of the fæces, constipation, uneasiness in the region of the stomach, loss of appetite, and general languor and… | To affect with jaundice; to color by prejudice or envy; to prejudice. The envy of wealth jaundiced his soul. Ld. Lytton.
jahvism: 1. The religion or worship of Yahweh (Jehovah), or the system of doctrines, etc., connected with it. 2. Use of Yahweh as a name of God.
jaspe: Having the surface decorated with cloudings and streaks, somewhat as if imitating jasper.
jalousie: A Venetian or slatted inside window blind.
janitor: A door-keeper; a porter; one who has the care of a public building, or a building occupied for offices, suites of rooms, etc.
jag: 1. A notch; a cleft; a barb; a ragged or sharp protuberance; a denticulation. Arethuss arose . . . From rock and from jag. Shelley. Garments thus beset with long jags. Holland. 2. A part broken off; | To cut into notches or teeth like those of a saw; to notch. [Written also jagg. Jagging iron, a wheel with a zigzag or jagged edge for cutting cakes or pastry into ornamental figures.
jacketing: The material of a jacket; as, nonconducting jacketing.
jaundiced: 1. affected with jaundice. Jaundiced eyes seem to see all objects yellow. Bp. Hall. 2. Prejudiced; envious; as, a jaundiced judgment.
jackstay: A rail of wood or iron stretching along a yard of a vessel, to which the sails are fastened.
jacamar: Any one of numerous species of tropical American birds of the genus Galbula and allied genera. They are allied to the kingfishers, but climb on tree trunks like nuthatches, and feed upon insects. Their colors are often brilliant.
jackstraw: 1. An effigy stuffed with straw; a scarecrow; hence, a man without property or influence. Milton. 2. One of a set of straws of strips of ivory, bone, wood, etc., for playing a child's game, the jackstraws being thrown confusedly together on a table, to be gathered up singly by a hooked instrument, without touching or disturbing the rest of the pile. See Spilikin.
jacent: Lying at length; as, the jacent posture. Sir H. Wotton.
jackadandy: A little dandy; a little, foppish, impertinent fellow.
jaculate: To throw or cast, as a dart; to throw out; to emit.
jazel: A gem of an azure color. (old)
